Machu Picchu. A fifteenth-century Inca citadel set high in the Andes mountains of Peru, built at the height of Inca imperial power. Hidden from Spanish conquistadors during the colonial conquest, it remained unknown to the outside world until 1911, and its remote mountain location and sophisticated stone construction make it one of the most iconic symbols of Inca engineering and civilization.

Located at two thousand four hundred thirty meters—nearly eight thousand feet—above sea level on a mountain ridge above the Urubamba River valley in southeastern Peru, Machu Picchu was built around 1450 CE during the reign of Pachacuti, the Inca emperor who expanded the empire to its greatest territorial extent. The Spanish conquistadors never found it during their campaigns in the sixteenth century, allowing it to remain hidden and undisturbed for nearly four hundred years.

The site is constructed without mortar; fitted stones are so precisely aligned that a knife blade cannot be inserted between them, demonstrating mastery of Inca architecture and engineering. The complex contains temples, residences, storage structures, and agricultural terraces built into the mountainside, suggesting it served as a royal estate or sacred ceremonial site of great importance.

The site was rediscovered in 1911 by American historian Hiram Bingham, whose work brought it to international attention and initiated systematic excavation. Today, the Inca Trail—a four-day hiking route connecting nearby Inca sites to Machu Picchu—remains one of the world's most famous treks, allowing visitors to experience the landscape that the Inca civilization transformed into one of the New World's greatest achievements and most enduring monuments to the empire that built it.
